sentences.text: Before writing a single line of model code, you need a working environment.
sentences.reason: Introductory framing sentence with no factual claim.

sentences.text: This chapter walks through every tool you will need throughout the book: PyTorch for tensor operations and training, tiktoken for tokenization, TensorFlow (briefly) for loading pre-trained GPT-2 weights, tqdm for download progress tracking, and Ollama for running open-source LLMs locally during evaluation.
sentences.reason: Overview/roadmap sentence describing chapter contents; no specific factual claim requiring citation.

sentences.text: Getting these pieces in place now will save you from interruptions later.
sentences.reason: Motivational statement; no factual claim.

sentences.text: One of the first decisions your code must make at runtime is which hardware device to use for computation.
sentences.reason: Introductory framing for the device selection section.

sentences.text: PyTorch supports three backends that are relevant here: CPU, CUDA (for NVIDIA GPUs), and MPS (Metal Performance Shaders, for Macs with Apple Silicon chips) [c2307].
sentences.reason: c2307 states the device can be CPU, CUDA for GPUs, or MPS for Macs with Apple silicon chips, which directly supports this sentence.

sentences.text: The standard one-liner for selecting between CPU and CUDA is:
sentences.reason: Introductory phrase before code block; no factual claim.

sentences.text: device = torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')
sentences.reason: c2309 contains this exact code.

sentences.text: If you are on a MacBook with an Apple Silicon chip, you can go one step further and set the device to `torch.device('mps')` for faster execution [c2310].
sentences.reason: c2310 states that for MacBooks with Apple silicon chips, the device can be set to torch.device('mps') for faster execution.

sentences.text: Apple Silicon is approximately 2× faster than the Apple CPU for these workloads [c3861], so it is worth the extra line if you have the hardware.
sentences.reason: c3861 states Apple silicon is approximately 2x faster than Apple CPU.

sentences.text: Intuitively, the device variable is passed around to every tensor and model call so that all computation happens in the same memory space.
sentences.reason: Explanatory statement about how device variables work; general technical explanation without specific factual claim requiring citation.

sentences.text: Mixing devices — for example, keeping your model on GPU while your data stays on CPU — is a common source of runtime errors, so it pays to establish a consistent device selection strategy early.
sentences.reason: General technical advice and motivation; no specific factual claim requiring citation.

sentences.text: A subtle but important optimization concerns *when* you transfer tensors to the target device.
sentences.reason: Introductory framing for the optimization discussion.

sentences.text: The recommended approach is to perform the device transfer inside a custom collate function, which runs as part of the data loading pipeline rather than inside the training loop [c2306, c2308].
sentences.reason: c2306 is a design_decision about custom collate function including code to move tensors to device. c2308 is a design_decision about performing device transfer in custom collate function. Both support this sentence.

sentences.text: Because the collate function executes in background worker processes, the transfer happens concurrently with the forward and backward passes, preventing it from blocking the GPU during model training [c2308].
sentences.reason: c2308 states that performing device transfer in the custom collate function allows the transfer to happen as a background process, preventing it from blocking the GPU during model training.

sentences.text: Later in the book you will load the original GPT-2 weights released by OpenAI.
sentences.reason: Forward-looking statement about future content; no factual claim requiring citation.

sentences.text: There is a small compatibility wrinkle: OpenAI originally saved those weights using TensorFlow, while the code in this series uses PyTorch [c3469].
sentences.reason: c3469 states OpenAI originally saved GPT-2 weights using TensorFlow, while the lecture series code uses PyTorch.

sentences.text: The weights therefore cannot be loaded directly with `torch.load`; TensorFlow must be installed as an intermediary [c3470].
sentences.reason: c3470 states TensorFlow must be installed to load the GPT-2 weights, which were originally saved in TensorFlow format.

sentences.text: Once you have trained or fine-tuned a model, you will want to compare its outputs against a strong reference.
sentences.reason: Motivational framing for the Ollama section.

sentences.text: Ollama is a lightweight application designed to run large language models on a laptop [c648].
sentences.reason: c648 defines Ollama as an efficient application to run large language models on your laptop.

sentences.text: It supports several well-known open-source models, including:
sentences.reason: Introductory phrase before a list; no factual claim.

sentences.text: **Llama 3** by Meta [c649]
sentences.reason: c649 states Ollama supports running LLAMA 3, developed by Meta.

sentences.text: **Phi 3** by Microsoft [c650]
sentences.reason: c650 states Ollama supports running Phi 3, developed by Microsoft.

sentences.text: **Mistral** [c651]
sentences.reason: c651 states Ollama supports running Mistral.
c652 states Ollama supports running Gemma 2.

sentences.text: An important distinction: Ollama is an inference-only tool [c657].
sentences.reason: c657 defines Ollama as a tool for generating text using LLM inference and does not support training or fine-tuning LLMs.

sentences.text: You perform inference with an already pre-trained model; Ollama does not support training or fine-tuning [c653, c657].
sentences.reason: c653 states using Ollama, you perform inference only, not pre-training; the model is already pre-trained. c657 states Ollama does not support training or fine-tuning LLMs.

sentences.text: Think of it as a convenient local server for querying models, not a training framework.
sentences.reason: Explanatory analogy; no factual claim requiring citation.

sentences.text: Ollama is available for Mac OS, Linux, and Windows [c658].
sentences.reason: c658 states Ollama is available for download on Mac OS, Linux, and Windows.

sentences.text: The Mac OS installer weighs in at 177 MB [c659], so the download is quick.
sentences.reason: c659 states the Ollama Mac OS installer file is 177 MB.

sentences.text: The model files themselves are a different story — the Llama 3 8-billion-parameter model is 4.7 GB [c664] and takes roughly 15 to 20 minutes to download on a typical connection [c665].
sentences.reason: c664 states the LLAMA 3 model files downloaded through Ollama are 4.7 GB in size. c665 states downloading the LLAMA 3 8 billion parameter model through Ollama takes approximately 15 to 20 minutes.

sentences.text: On Mac, a single terminal command downloads (on first run) and starts the model:

sentences.text: When Ollama has successfully loaded Llama 3, right-hand-side arrows appear in the terminal, indicating the model is ready for interaction [c666].

sentences.text: On Windows the process requires two commands in sequence: first start the server, then launch the model [c663].

sentences.text: Then, in the same or a second terminal:

sentences.text: A good habit is to open a dedicated terminal tab for Ollama and leave it untouched while you work in other tabs.
